# @kcc/lms

A learning-management module: courses, cohorts, modules, lessons, progress and
assessments. Built to be merged into an application that already exists rather
than run as one.

**Runs on MySQL or PostgreSQL.** One set of rules, two data layers, and the
same 142-check probe suite runs against both engines — which is the only
reason that claim is worth anything.

It owns **thirteen tables, all prefixed `lms_`**, and knows nothing about the
host beyond what `src/ports.ts` asks for. There is no framework in here, no
session library, no storage client and no HTTP. You keep your own auth, your
own routing, your own UI.

---

## What you get, and what you don't

**You get** the data model, the migration, and the service layer: the rules
about who may see what, how progress is recorded, how a quiz is scored. That
is the part that is tedious to get right and quiet when it is wrong.

**You don't get** screens. There are no React components, no CSS and no
routes, because we don't know what your application is built with and a
component carrying someone else's design tokens is not a thing you can merge.
`examples/next-app-router/` has reference route handlers if you happen to be
on Next.js — copy them, don't depend on them.

### What we assumed about your application

We have not seen it. These are the assumptions, and each one says what to do
if it is wrong:

| Assumption | If not |
|---|---|
| **MySQL 8.0.4+ or PostgreSQL 13+** | Both are supported and tested. MySQL 5.7 works except the topic filter on the catalogue, which needs `JSON_TABLE`. SQLite or SQL Server would need a third schema and a third store; the rules would not change. |
| **A `users` table keyed by a UUID** | Change three columns and their `references` clauses. See *The one seam*, below. |
| **On MySQL, a connection in UTC** | Not optional — see *The one seam*. A connection in any other zone shifts every stored instant. |
| **TypeScript** | The schema and migrations are usable from any language; the service layer is not. |
| **Drizzle, or willing to add it** | The migrations are plain SQL and work with any ORM. The services talk to a `Store` interface, and the bundled implementation uses Drizzle — which can sit alongside Prisma or TypeORM against the same database. On neither, implement `Store` yourself: forty-odd methods, none of them clever, and every rule comes with it. |

---

## Installing

```bash
# as a path dependency, a git dependency, or vendored into your repo
npm install ./vendor/kcc-lms          # or: npm i github:paulsendrake/KCLMS
```

Peer dependencies: `drizzle-orm`, plus `mysql2` **or** `pg` for whichever
engine you are on.

Then apply the migration for your engine:

```bash
mysql "$DATABASE" < migrations/mysql/0001_lms.sql        # MySQL
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -f migrations/postgres/0001_lms.sql  # PostgreSQL
```

Both are idempotent, so either is safe from a boot hook as well as a release
step. If you apply the MySQL file with your own tooling, read the note in
`migrations/README.md` about how it splits statements — the obvious split
silently skips the first table.

### The one seam

Three columns reference your user table:

```
lms_cohort_members.user_id
lms_lesson_progress.user_id
lms_quiz_attempts.user_id
```

They are declared against `users (id)` — `uuid` on Postgres, `char(36)` on
MySQL. If your table has another name, or keys people by `bigint` or `text`,
edit those three columns in `migrations/<engine>/0001_lms.sql` and in
`src/schema/<engine>.ts` if you use the Drizzle definitions. Nothing else in
the module reaches outside itself.

The module reads **no column but `id`** and never writes to your user table, so
everything else about your user model is invisible to it.

### On MySQL: the connection must be in UTC

```ts
createPool({ uri: process.env.DATABASE_URL, timezone: 'Z' })
```

MySQL's `TIMESTAMP` converts to and from the session's time zone, so a
connection in any other zone reads back a different instant than it wrote.
This is not a preference: it is the difference between a course release date
that opens a course when it should and one that opens it hours early, with
nothing in the data to show why.

Two more MySQL notes, both already handled but worth knowing:

- **Ids are generated by the application, not the database.** MySQL has no
  `RETURNING`, so an insert cannot hand back a generated key. Both dialects
  mint ids in TypeScript so there is one code path rather than two. (MariaDB
  *does* have `RETURNING` — relying on it would pass every test and fail on
  real MySQL.)
- **Search is case-insensitive because your collation says so.** MySQL has no
  `ILIKE`; a plain `LIKE` folds case under the default collations. If your
  columns use a `_bin` collation, search becomes case-sensitive.

## Wiring it up

```ts
import { lmsContext, asViewer, mysqlStore, myCourses, getLesson, completeLesson } from '@kcc/lms';

// Once, at startup. `postgresStore` for Postgres — nothing else changes.
const store = mysqlStore({ db });

const ports = {
  storage: { signedUrl: (key, ttl) => s3.sign(key, ttl) },
  video:   { playback: (ref) => mux.token(ref) },
  notifier: { notify: (event) => queue.push(event) },
};

// Per request, with the viewer from your own session.
const lms = lmsContext({ store, viewer: asViewer(user.id, user.role), ports });

const shelf = await myCourses(lms);
const lesson = await getLesson(lms, 'foundations', 'first-lesson');
await completeLesson(lms, lesson.id);
```

`db` is your existing Drizzle handle. `asViewer` maps your role string onto the
module's three — `learner`, `instructor`, `admin` — and if your roles don't
resemble those, write the four-line mapping yourself rather than bending to it.
**A wrong mapping here is an authorisation bug, and it is the one kind this
module cannot catch for you.**

All four ports are optional. With none of them you get courses, lessons,
progress and quizzes; attachments and video are withheld rather than broken,
and nothing is notified.

### Errors

Typed, so you can map them to responses without matching on message text:
`LmsForbidden`, `LmsNotFound`, `LmsInvalid`, `LmsConflict`. `LmsForbidden`
means the viewer is not entitled — render it as a refusal.

---

## The rule the whole thing turns on

**A learner may open a course only through a cohort they belong to, which that
course has been released to, on or after its release date.**

Four conditions. Leaving any one of them out shows somebody coursework they
were never given, so it is answered in exactly one place —
`entitlement()` in `src/services/enrolment.ts` — and every other service asks
that one rather than rebuilding the join.

```ts
const state = await entitlement(lms, courseId);
// { allowed: true,  reason: 'cohort' | 'staff', cohortIds: [...] }
// { allowed: false, reason: 'not_enrolled' | 'not_published' | 'no_such_course' }
// { allowed: false, reason: 'not_yet', availableFrom: Date }
```

It returns the reason because your screens need it: *"opens on the 14th"* and
*"you are not enrolled on this"* are different things to tell somebody.

Instructors and admins are exempt, deliberately and in one place, because they
author and mark the material.

**If you add a new way to read course material, call `requireEntitlement()`
first and add it to `DOORS` in `scripts/probe-entitlement.ts`.** An access rule
enforced on four screens out of five is not enforced, and that list is what
stops the fifth being forgotten.

### Don't query the tables directly

Read through the services. The moment a screen writes its own join against
`lms_lessons`, the entitlement rule stops being the only answer to "may this
person see this" — and the second answer is the one that will be wrong.

---

## What is actually in here

| Area | File | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Access | `services/enrolment.ts` | Cohorts, membership, releasing courses, `entitlement()` |
| Reading | `services/learning.ts` | A learner's shelf, course outline, a lesson, progress percentages |
| Catalogue | `services/catalogue.ts` | Browsing and searching published courses, paged, with facets |
| Progress | `services/progress.ts` | Watched seconds, completion, undo |
| Assessment | `services/assessment.ts` | Quiz papers, scoring, attempt limits |
| Authoring | `services/authoring.ts` | Courses, modules, lessons, attachments, quizzes |
| Ports | `ports.ts` | What the module needs from your application |
| Data | `store.ts` | Every database operation, in domain terms |
| Engines | `stores/drizzle.ts`, `stores/dialect.ts` | One implementation of `Store`; the five places the dialects differ |

### How two databases are supported without two codebases

The services never touch a table. They call `Store` (`src/store.ts`), which
describes every database operation in domain terms, and one implementation
satisfies it for both engines. The genuine dialect differences — upsert
spelling, case-insensitive `LIKE`, JSON containment, unnesting a JSON array,
casting a count — are five functions in `src/stores/dialect.ts`.

Two copies of the services, one per engine, was the obvious alternative and is
rejected: the rules are the product, and two copies of a rule is one rule
about to be wrong on one engine. What keeps this honest is that the whole
probe suite runs against both, so a rule that stops being shared fails twice.

A few decisions worth knowing before you build screens on it:

- **A course cannot be born published.** `createCourse` ignores any status and
  writes a draft; publishing is a separate admin-only call. And a course with
  no published lesson cannot be published at all, or a learner opens an empty
  outline and reads it as the platform being broken.
- **Quiz papers carry no answer key.** `getQuizPaper()` returns no
  `isCorrect` and no explanations — not filtered out, but never selected. The
  correct answers appear only in the result of a submitted attempt. Scoring
  happens server-side from the stored options; the client sends only which
  option it chose.
- **An unanswered question is wrong, not skipped.** Otherwise leaving out the
  questions you don't know raises your percentage.
- **Watched seconds only go up.** Players post progress every few seconds and
  it arrives out of order; a late packet must not rewind somebody's progress.
- **Progress percentages count published lessons only**, so publishing a new
  lesson never looks like losing progress already earned.
- **Lesson bodies are returned as data, never rendered.** `bodyFormat` tells
  you whether it is Markdown or HTML. Render Markdown to elements rather than
  to HTML, and sanitise HTML — or a lesson author can put a script tag in
  front of a cohort.

## Probes

```bash
# PostgreSQL
createdb lms_probe
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/lms_probe npm run probe:pg

# MySQL
mysql -e 'create database lms_probe'
ENGINE=mysql DATABASE_URL=mysql://user:pass@127.0.0.1/lms_probe npm run probe

# or both, which is what counts
npm run probe:both
```

Five suites, **142 checks on each engine**, run against a real database — the
rules here *are* joins, unique indexes and upserts, so a mocked database would
be a test of the mock. Each probe creates a stand-in `users` table and applies
the migration, so **point it at a scratch database.**

Every rule above was verified by breaking it on purpose and confirming the
right check fails. Eight rule mutations, all caught: dropping the release-date
condition from `entitlement()`; dropping the published-status condition;
letting the list query drift from the single-course check; sending the answer
key with the paper; scoring only answered questions; letting watched seconds be
overwritten; dropping the catalogue's sort tiebreak; and un-escaping the LIKE
wildcards.

Four more on the dialect layer: crossing the MySQL tables with the Postgres
dialect; giving MySQL the Postgres upsert; misreading mysql2's
`[rows, fields]` tuple as a row count; and — the one that proves the
architecture — dropping a rule from the shared decision function, which fails
**identically on both engines**.

`probe-entitlement.ts` is the one to read first.

### What the probes were run against

PostgreSQL 16 and **MariaDB 10.11**, which is what this build environment can
install. MariaDB is close to MySQL but not identical, so the module avoids
every MariaDB-only feature it might otherwise have leaned on — `RETURNING`
above all, which MariaDB has and MySQL does not, and which would therefore
have passed every test here and failed on your database. Worth a run against
your actual MySQL before you rely on it; `npm run probe` against a scratch
schema is the whole check.

---

## Provenance

Extracted from the Kingdom Connections platform, where this ran as part of a
larger application on PostgreSQL. What was removed in the extraction: the 7
Mountains taxonomy, the Cloudflare Stream and R2 clients (now the `video` and
`storage` ports), the notification system (now the `notifier` port), the AI
curriculum-draft generator, and all session and role handling (now `Viewer`).

Table names gained their `lms_` prefix here, so this is not drop-in compatible
with that database — it is the same model, not the same deployment.
